title: Heart Surgeon Warns Smoking, Vaping Damage the Body 'From Top to Toes'
excerpt: Board-certified cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Jeremy London says smoking in any form — tobacco, marijuana or vaping — is "the single worst thing you can do for your entire body," urging smokers to get help and those around them to offer support.
body:
• In a September 14 Instagram video, board-certified cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Jeremy London called smoking and vaping "the single worst thing you can do for your entire body."
  • Inhaled smoke, he explained, floods the bloodstream with toxic chemicals, tar and carbon monoxide, attacking the inner lining of blood vessels and cutting off oxygen and nutrients "from the top of the head to the tip of the toes."
  • His warning covers tobacco, marijuana and vaping alike: "Lungs have one function. Good air in, bad air out. Everything else is toxic."
  • Quitting is hard, he acknowledged, but the body begins to recover within 20 minutes of the last cigarette — "the single most important lever you can pull for your entire health."

The cigarette you light after a long day may feel like relief, but a heart surgeon with 25 years of operating-room experience says the damage reaches far beyond the lungs. In an Instagram video shared on September 14, Dr Jeremy London, a board-certified cardiothoracic surgeon, laid out why he considers smoking and vaping "the single worst thing you can do for your body" — and why quitting may be the most consequential health decision a smoker can make.

Dr London is known for blunt, prevention-focused health takes, including an earlier list of habits he personally avoids with smoking ranked at the top. His latest video details how inhaled smoke travels through the body.

How smoke moves beyond the lungs

The lungs, Dr London explains, have one job: taking in oxygen and expelling carbon dioxide. Inhaling anything else — tobacco, marijuana or vapor — introduces substances they were never built to handle.

"Smoking anything, marijuana, vaping, cigarettes, is the single worst thing you can do for your entire body. It affects every organ. Let's start with the lungs. Lungs have one function. Good air in, bad air out. Everything else is toxic."

— Dr Jeremy London, cardiothoracic surgeon

The damage does not stop there. According to Dr London, smoke floods the bloodstream with toxic chemicals, tar and carbon monoxide. These attack the inner lining of the blood vessels, causing blockages that impair the delivery of oxygen and nutrients "to the entire body from the top of the head to the tip of the toes."

For people who already have heart disease or a tendency toward atherosclerosis — the hardening and narrowing of arteries — the risk is compounded. As he told TODAY.com in an earlier interview, smoking "actually accelerates that process exponentially."

Vaping under scrutiny

Dr London has been particularly vocal about vaping, which many users treat as a safer alternative. Research cited in coverage of his advice suggests vapers show "worrisome changes" in heart and blood vessel function, and he has previously described himself as being on a "personal crusade" against vaping after treating young patients with devastating lung injuries linked to it — cases severe enough to require ECMO, an external lung machine, according to a transcript of his appearance on the Mel Robbins podcast.

Because vaping's long-term effects are still being studied, he argues the uncertainty itself is a reason for caution: the exposure is continuous and the nicotine content in many products is unregulated and highly addictive.

Why quitting still pays off — fast

Tobacco and nicotine addiction is real, and Dr London does not minimize it. Quitting can trigger intense cravings, mood changes, sleep problems and increased appetite. But the recovery clock starts quickly: the body begins to repair itself within 20 minutes of the last cigarette.

"I understand it's hard. I get that. But stopping smoking is the single most important lever you can pull for your entire health. If you smoke, get the help you need to quit."

— Dr Jeremy London, cardiothoracic surgeon

His advice to those around smokers is equally direct: offer support, not judgment.

Why this lands differently for the diaspora

For South Asian diaspora communities, the warning has a particular resonance. Tobacco use in these communities extends beyond cigarettes — hookah, bidis and smokeless forms like gutka and paan masala are familiar in many households and social settings, and are sometimes left out of conversations about smoking. Dr London's warning covers every inhaled form, which puts hookah and bidi use squarely in the same frame, while his vaping alarm speaks to younger users who may consider e-cigarettes harmless.

What's next

For smokers, the practical takeaway is to seek structured help — counseling, quitlines and clinician support improve the odds of quitting far more than willpower alone. For everyone else, Dr London's message is to support, not shame, the people trying to stop. As he puts it, no other single change does more for the whole body.

Note: This article summarizes a social media video and is for informational purposes only. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice.
image_caption: A metal ashtray filled with extinguished cigarette butts. Heart surgeon Dr Jeremy London warns that smoking and vaping in any form is the single worst thing for the body, damaging blood vessels and organs from the top of the head to the tip of the toes.
nri_angle: South Asian diaspora tobacco use spans hookah, bidis and smokeless forms often left out of smoking conversations; Dr London's all-inhaled-forms warning and vaping alarm speak directly to those blind spots.
